section_summary: This section comprises diplomatic despatches, cross-reference sheets, telegrams, and private correspondence regarding Japanese internal affairs, military trials, and political mobilization from August 1937 to March 1938. Key documents detail the court-martial sentencing of civilian ringleaders Zei Nishida and Kazuteru Kita and the acquittal of General Jinzaburo Mazaki in connection with the February 26, 1936 uprising. Comprehensive embassy reporting examines the decline of parliamentary party politics, the December 1937 police roundup of labor and leftist figures including Kanju Kato and Baroness Shizue Ishimoto, and severe parliamentary friction over the National Mobilization Bill. Additional materials report rising anti-British sentiment, high-level civil-military policy conferences, and official New Year proclamations bracing the Japanese public for protracted conflict and state economic controls.

subfiles.about: W. L. Godfrey forwards an alleged strategic map of the Pacific area to President Roosevelt in light of the Sino-Japanese conflict.
subfiles.summary: W. L. Godfrey of the W. L. Godfrey Agency in San Francisco sends a letter to President Franklin D. Roosevelt enclosing a strategic map of the Pacific area. Godfrey explains that he obtained the document several years earlier from an employee who had served with Canadian forces in Siberia and worked eighteen years as a Chinese interpreter at Angel Island. He offers the map to the administration for whatever utility it may have regarding the current conflict in China and asks for its return if not needed. Godfrey also includes personal references to his son employed at the government depot in Jeffersonville, Indiana, and his sister working at the post office in Mitchell, Indiana.
subfiles.title: Letter from W. L. Godfrey to President Franklin D. Roosevelt Enclosing Pacific Strategic Map

subfiles.about: The Department of State returns an examined strategic map of the Pacific area to W. L. Godfrey.
subfiles.summary: Writing on behalf of the Secretary of State, Maxwell M. Hamilton, Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, acknowledges receipt of W. L. Godfrey's letter of August 20, 1937, referred by the White House. Hamilton states that the document purporting to be a strategic map of the Pacific area has been carefully examined by the Department. In accordance with Godfrey's request, the map is returned to him with an expression of appreciation for his courtesy in submitting it.
subfiles.title: Letter from Maxwell M. Hamilton to W. L. Godfrey Returning Pacific Area Map

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports court-martial sentences handed down against civilian participants in the February 26, 1936 insurrection.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports that on August 14, 1937, the Tokyo Court Martial sentenced civilian ringleaders Zei Nishida and Kazuteru Kita to death for their leadership in the February 26, 1936 insurrection. Civilian defendants Tetsuya Kamekawa and Teruo Nakabashi were sentenced to life imprisonment and three years' imprisonment, respectively. The War Ministry announcement disclosed that part of Nishida's conspiracy involved asking General Jinzaburo Mazaki to head a new military government due to the plotters' deep respect for him. Grew cross-references earlier embassy despatches regarding the trial and arrest of General Mazaki.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2551: Court Martial Sentences for the Civilian Participants in the February 26 Insurrection

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a report from Kobe transmitting a letter to the Ambassador on military and political matters.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Despatch No. 152 from Consul Winthrop R. Scott at Kobe, dated August 11, 1937. The despatch transmits a copy of a letter written to American Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo concerning military and political developments in Japan. The underlying paper is indexed under decimal file classification 894.20/181.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Despatch No. 152 from Kobe Regarding Military and Political Matters

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a letter from Kobe to Ambassador Grew regarding political and military conditions.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Despatch No. 153 dated August 13, 1937, from Consul Winthrop R. Scott at Kobe. The communication forwards a copy of a letter sent to Ambassador Grew reporting on political and military matters in Japan. The permanent document is filed under decimal classification 894.20/180.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Despatch No. 153 from Kobe Regarding Military and Political Matters

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 154 from Kobe reporting on military and political developments.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 154, dated August 17, 1937, submitted by Consul Winthrop R. Scott from Kobe. The despatch encloses a letter reporting to Ambassador Grew on military and political matters in the Kobe consular district. The original paper is filed under classification 894.20/182.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Despatch No. 154 from Kobe Regarding Military and Political Matters

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 165 from Kobe enclosing a report on political and military affairs.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Despatch No. 165 dated September 13, 1937, from Consul Winthrop R. Scott in Kobe. The despatch forwards copies of Scott's letter of the same date addressed to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo concerning political and military conditions in Kobe. The document is indexed under file number 894.20/184.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Despatch No. 165 from Kobe Regarding Political and Military Matters in Kobe

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 164 from Kobe submitting a confidential report on political and military affairs.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 164 dated September 10, 1937, from Consul Winthrop R. Scott at Kobe. It records the submission of copies of a confidential report sent to Ambassador Grew concerning political and military conditions in Japan. The original communication is preserved under file number 894.20/183.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Despatch No. 164 from Kobe Submitting Confidential Report

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports the court-martial acquittal of General Mazaki and encloses a newspaper account detailing the tribunal's findings.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports that the Tokyo Court Martial acquitted General Jinzaburo Mazaki on September 25, 1937, on grounds of insufficient evidence to prove that he actively aided rebels during the February 26, 1936 uprising. Grew analyzes the official judgment, pointing out that the court established Mazaki's extensive knowledge of the conspiracy, his resentment over his removal as Inspector General of Military Education, and his expressions of moral sympathy with the young insurgent officers. Grew suggests that Mazaki was acquitted to avert domestic political complications during the ongoing national emergency, and notes that condemned civilian ringleaders Zei Nishida and Kazuteru Kita were executed on August 19. An enclosed clipping from The Japan Advertiser provides a full Domei translation of the court-martial's statement of reasons and historical background on the uprising.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2608: Court Martial and Acquittal of General Mazaki

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Telegram No. 509 regarding government reorganization for a total war footing.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Telegram No. 509 sent at 2 p.m. on November 2, 1937, by Ambassador Joseph C. Grew in Tokyo. The telegram reports on proposed changes within the Japanese government machinery aimed at placing the nation on as complete a wartime basis as possible. The underlying communication is catalogued under decimal classification 793.94 Conference/163.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Telegram No. 509 from Tokyo on Political Affairs and War Basis

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Despatch No. 184 from Kobe transmitting a report to Ambassador Grew on military matters.
subfiles.summary: This document file note indexes Despatch No. 184 dated October 23, 1937, from Consul Winthrop R. Scott at Kobe. The despatch forwards a report addressed to Ambassador Grew in Tokyo concerning military developments within the Kobe district. The paper is filed under classification 894.20/191.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Despatch No. 184 from Kobe Regarding Military Matters

subfiles.about: Chargé Leonard transmits a press summary of an essay by Estonian writer A. H. Tammsaare analyzing Japan's geopolitical trajectory and rivalry with the United States.
subfiles.summary: Walter A. Leonard, American Chargé d'Affaires a.i. in Tallinn, transmits a résumé of an essay entitled 'Japan and the Japanese' published in the Estonian press by novelist A. H. Tammsaare (pen name of Anton Hansen). Leonard explains that the article is part of a five-part series on Japanese society, economics, and foreign policy, and confirms with the Estonian Foreign Office that it carries no official sponsorship or endorsement. The enclosed summary reviews Japan's emergence as an imperial power since Commodore Perry, historical grievances over the Portsmouth Treaty, dissatisfaction with the Washington naval ratios, and the construction of Pacific island bases. Tammsaare argues that Japan views the United States as its ultimate geopolitical rival and is invading China to secure vital raw materials and industrial self-sufficiency before an inevitable conflict with America.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 290: Transmitting Resumé of an Article on Japan by A. H. Tammsaare in the Estonian Press

subfiles.about: Consul Scott reports frank comments made by Japanese diplomat Fumio Miura regarding intense anti-British feeling and Japan's determination in China.
subfiles.summary: Consul Winthrop R. Scott transmits a confidential report detailing frank statements made by Fumio Miura of the Japanese Foreign Office during a private luncheon hosted by the Brazilian Consul General in Kobe. Miura stressed that intense anti-British sentiment was sweeping Japan, arguing that Britain was actively supporting Nanking financially and morally to preserve its Asiatic interests by pitting China against Japan. Miura discounted President Roosevelt's Chicago address as domestic rhetoric, expressed bitter contempt for the Brussels Conference, and stated unequivocally that Japan would settle the China conflict without outside interference in what promised to be a protracted war. A State Department minute sheet dated December 2 highlights the value of Miura's candid views in confirming Japanese hostility toward Britain and contempt for international intervention.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 189: Political Matters in Kobe, Japan (Reporting Remarks of Fumio Miura)

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits detailed revisions and updated data on Japanese political institutions and parties for the Council on Foreign Relations.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a copy of his response to Walter H. Mallory, Executive Director of the Council on Foreign Relations, providing revised and updated material on Japan for the Political Handbook of the World. The enclosure provides comprehensive information on the Japanese constitution, the structure of the Imperial Diet, and the formation of the cabinet under Prince Fumimaro Konoe following the dissolution under General Senjuro Hayashi. It presents detailed political analyses of the major parliamentary parties—the Minseito, Seiyukai, Shakai Taishuto, Kokumin Domei, and Tohokai—including their ideological platforms, historical evolution, prominent leadership, and seat totals after the April 1937 general election. The document also contains a descriptive catalog of Japan's major metropolitan and regional daily newspapers, English-language journals, and news agencies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2650: Material for Political Handbook of the World

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a report from Kobe on military affairs and efforts to improve Anglo-Japanese relations.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records a despatch dated November 18, 1937, from Consul Winthrop R. Scott at Kobe. The despatch forwards a letter addressed to the Tokyo Embassy reporting on military developments in Kobe and notes that diplomatic efforts were being made to improve relations between Japan and Great Britain. The original document is classified under decimal file 894.20/195.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Despatch from Kobe on Military Matters and Anglo-Japanese Relations

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports joint government and Imperial Headquarters conferences and assesses that a declaration of war is not imminent.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports that high-level conferences between the Japanese government and Imperial Headquarters have been underway since December 14 to determine major national policies. He notes that if a consensus is reached, the Cabinet plans to request that the Emperor convene an Imperial conference in the near future. Grew informs the Department that despite widespread press speculation, confidential information leads him to believe that a formal declaration of war against China is not imminent. A Document File Note indexing the telegram under file 793.94/11664 precedes the text on page 415.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 644: Government and Imperial Headquarters Deliberations on National Policy

subfiles.about: Correspondence and newspaper clippings concerning the detention and release of feminist leader Baroness Shizue Ishimoto by Tokyo police.
subfiles.summary: Mrs. W. B. Cannon of Cambridge, Massachusetts, writes to the Department of State on December 28, 1937, inquiring whether any diplomatic representations can be made on behalf of her friend, prominent author and feminist Baroness Shizue Ishimoto, following news of her arrest in Tokyo. Joseph W. Ballantine, Acting Chief of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs, responds on January 5, 1938, informing Mrs. Cannon that according to a Tokyo press despatch, Baroness Ishimoto was released on December 30. Enclosed news clippings from the Associated Press and a feature cable by Hugh Byas in The New York Times report that Baroness Ishimoto was detained for two weeks and interrogated by the Metropolitan Police 'dangerous thoughts' division regarding her birth control advocacy and leftist acquaintances before being released under orders not to leave Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Correspondence and Press Reports Regarding the Arrest and Release of Baroness Shizue Ishimoto

subfiles.about: Embassy Tokyo analyzes the historical evolution and decline of Japanese political parties and assesses the structural prerequisites for genuine representative democracy.
subfiles.summary: In an extensive political analysis drafted by Counselor Eugene H. Dooman, Ambassador Joseph C. Grew examines the collapse of constitutional party politics in Japan under wartime conditions. The despatch traces the history of Japanese political factions since the establishment of the Diet in 1890, highlighting how patronage networks, corrupt practices, and the loss of charismatic leadership discredited traditional parties like the Seiyukai and Minseito. Dooman explains that the real underlying conflict in Japan is between inherited medieval feudalism and modern thought, describing how recent efforts to forge a new two-party dynamic between the leftist Social Mass Party and right-wing nationalist groups led by Mitsuru Toyama were derailed by police roundups of labor leaders such as Kanju Kato. He concludes that a viable democratic two-party system will only emerge when mechanization creates a substantial class of educated factory artisans who can throw off feudal social ties. A Department of State summary memorandum by Langdon precedes the despatch.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2722: Trends in Japanese Party Politics

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew transmits and analyzes public New Year messages by Japanese Cabinet ministers and economic leaders forecasting national mobilization and protracted warfare.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reviews the annual New Year proclamations issued on January 1, 1938, by key Japanese government officials, observing an atmosphere of national confidence coupled with calls for total mobilization for a protracted struggle in China. Premier Fumimaro Konoe characterized 1938 as a transformative era requiring the organic marshaling of all national resources, while Foreign Minister Koki Hirota addressed tensions with Britain and the Soviet Union, the amicable settlement of the Panay incident, and closer ties with Germany and Italy. Home Minister Nobumasa Suetsugu warned of enduring international friction, and economic authorities—including Finance Minister Okinori Kaya, Bank of Japan Governor Toyotaro Yuki, Commerce Minister Shinji Yoshino, and Agriculture Minister Yoriyasu Arima—appealed for public consumption cutbacks, expansion of heavy industrial production, and rural economic rationalization to sustain wartime trade and bond financing. Six clippings from The Japan Advertiser reproducing the complete statements are enclosed.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2727: New Year Messages of Japanese Officials

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports parliamentary opposition to the government's draft National Mobilization Bill and assesses that it will likely pass after modification.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew transmits a confidential appraisal regarding parliamentary and public controversy over the draft National Mobilization Bill prepared by the National Planning Board and the Bureau of Legislation. Grew reports that political parties and liberal remnants in the Diet strongly oppose the sweeping transfer of control over productive industry to Imperial Headquarters and the executive's power to curtail private initiative by ordinance, with critics alleging the measure introduces authoritarian rule. However, Grew clarifies that opposition is focused on the vague and overly broad drafting of the measure rather than total resistance, and reports that a prominent Diet member expects the bill to pass after extensive amendments. A confidential State Department paraphrase of the telegram is included on pages 443–444.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 105: Opposition to the National Mobilization Bill

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports political compromises on the National Mobilization Bill, amendments to the electric power control measure, and moves to establish a single national party.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports that acute friction between the Japanese government and political parties over the National Mobilization Bill subsided following a late-night Cabinet meeting and conferences where the Minseito and Seiyukai renewed their support. Despite these assurances, the Lower House amended the government's priority Electric Power Control Bill in an unsatisfactory manner and maintained parliamentary delays against the mobilization bill in committee. Grew further reports that party leaders are weighing the merger of existing parties into a single national organization to prevent complete political extinction by an army-backed group, with observers expecting Prince Fumimaro Konoe to accept the leadership of the proposed unified party.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 159: Diet Developments on Mobilization, Electric Power Control, and Single Party Movement

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Ambassador Bullitt's conversations in Warsaw and Berlin regarding Japanese strategic aims in China and against the Soviet Union.
subfiles.summary: This document file note records Despatch No. 1267 dated November 23, 1937, from Ambassador William C. Bullitt in Paris, originally classified under 123 Bullitt, William C./382. The despatch details Bullitt's conversation in Warsaw with Japanese Ambassador Sakoh, who stated that no one in Tokyo understood current China policy and expressed personal hopes for a military withdrawal from Central and Southern China with peace based on autonomy for the northern provinces. The paper also summarizes Bullitt's conference in Berlin with General Hermann Göring, who asserted that Japan intended to organize North China as a strategic base for an inevitable war against the Soviet Union to neutralize Vladivostok.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet: Despatch No. 1267 from Paris on Ambassador Bullitt's Conversations in Warsaw and Berlin

subfiles.about: Ambassador Grew reports sharp conflict between the government and political parties in the Diet, violence by reactionaries, and parliamentary disruption.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Joseph C. Grew reports serious political friction in Tokyo as sessions of the Lower House of the Diet and parliamentary committees were marked by disorder and violent denunciations of the government for infringing personal liberties and private initiative. He recounts coercive incidents, including the physical occupation of political party headquarters by members of an anti-communist association without police intervention, and a violent assault against the leader of the Social Mass Party by a suspected reactionary. The telegram describes an appearance by an army officer before a Diet committee to defend the administration's policies as the transmission concludes at the bottom of the page.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 149: Disorder in the Diet and Clashes Between Government and Parties
